text: Question one. What kinds of bugs do AI assistants characteristically introduce? Code that is almost right. In Stack Overflow's twenty twenty-five developer survey, sixty-six percent of respondents named AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite, as their top frustration. Forty-five percent said debugging AI-generated code takes longer than expected. The usual suspects start at the edges. Boundaries: an off-by-one, a less-than where less-than-or-equal belongs, the empty input, the exact edge of a window. Unstated assumptions: input assumed sorted, unique, never null, or plain ask-ee. Invented APIs: a method, a parameter or a whole package that doesn't exist, or a real function called with the wrong signature. An invented package name is also a supply-chain risk, because an attacker can register it. Swallowed errors: a broad except that hides the failure the caller needed to see. And security: sequel built by string formatting, secrets pasted into the code, a missing authorization check. Two more live in the diff around the code. Tests that agree with the bug assert what the code does, not what it should do, so they pass and prove nothing. And scope creep: renamed variables, reformatted files and unrelated edits, slipped in beside the change. Notice which of them make a noise. An invented API fails as soon as its line runs, unless someone has registered the package. The other six run quietly and survive the happy path, so running the example proves very little. Three of them are in our diff.
